target_output:
You are exactly right about how color works for physical objects! When you look at a red apple, light (from the sun or a lamp) hits the apple, the apple absorbs most of the light, and it **reflects** only the red light back into your eyes. 

However, computer and TV screens work completely differently. Instead of *reflecting* light, they **emit (create) their own light**. 

Here is a breakdown of how they do it:

**1. Additive vs. Subtractive Color**
*   **Physical objects (Subtractive):** Paint, ink, and objects use "subtractive" color. If you mix all the colors of paint together, you get a dark, muddy brown/black. 
*   **Screens (Additive):** Screens use "additive" color. Because they are made of pure light, mixing colors works differently. If you mix all the colors of light together, you get pure white. 

**2. Pixels and Subpixels**
If you were to take a magnifying glass and look extremely closely at your computer screen, you would see that the image is made up of millions of tiny squares called **pixels**. 

Inside every single pixel, there are three even tinier lights called **subpixels**. These three lights are always the same colors: **Red, Green, and Blue (RGB)**. 

**3. The Illusion of Mixing**
These subpixels are so microscopic and packed so closely together that your human eye cannot see them individually. Instead, your brain blends them together into a single color. 

The screen creates all the colors you see by simply changing how bright each of those three little red, green, and blue lights are. 
*   If the screen wants to show **Red**, it turns the red light to 100%, and turns the green and blue lights off.
*   If it wants to show **Yellow**, it turns the red and green lights on to 100%, and leaves blue off. (Mixing red and green *light* makes yellow!)
*   If it wants to show **Purple**, it mixes red and blue.
*   If it wants to show pure **White**, it turns all three lights on to 100%. 
*   If it wants to show **Black**, it turns all three lights completely off.

By slightly adjusting the brightness of those three tiny lights on a scale from 0 to 100%, a single pixel can produce over 16 million different color combinations. 

**Why Red, Green, and Blue?**
Screens use these specific colors because of human biology. The back of your eye (the retina) contains microscopic light receptors called "cones." You have three types of cones: ones that are sensitive to red, ones sensitive to green, and ones sensitive to blue. 

Therefore, a TV screen doesn't actually need to create "real" yellow or purple light. It just shines the exact right amount of red, green, and blue light to "hack" your eyes and trick your brain into seeing those colors!

You have just hit on a really profound point, and from a biological perspective, **you are 100% correct.** 

From the perspective of your eyes and your brain, light is light. A photon is a photon. Your retina does not care whether a photon of red light bounced off an apple or was shot out of a glowing LED on your phone. Once that light enters your pupil, the biological process of seeing color is exactly the same. 

So, in terms of *human perception*, you are absolutely right: it is just light hitting your eyes. 

However, from the perspective of physics, art, and engineering, the "emit vs. reflect" distinction is definitely not just a technicality. It completely changes the rules of how color behaves in the real world. Here is why the difference actually matters:

**1. The "Pitch-Black Room" Test**
The most obvious difference is how the object interacts with its environment. 
*   If you take a red apple into a pitch-black room, it ceases to be red. It is black. It has no color of its own, because its color is entirely dependent on borrowing light from the environment. 
*   If you take your phone screen into a pitch-black room, it is still brilliantly colorful. It brings its own energy to the equation. 

**2. The "Fake Yellow" vs. "Real Yellow"**
This is where the physics get really wild. 
If you look at a yellow banana in the sunlight, the banana is absorbing other colors and reflecting **actual, physical yellow light waves** (which have a wavelength of about 580 nanometers) into your eye. 

If you look at a yellow banana on your computer screen, **there is zero yellow light hitting your eye.** The screen is actually shooting Red light (650 nanometers) and Green light (530 nanometers) at you at the exact same time. 

Because of that biological "hack" mentioned earlier, your brain processes the combination of Red and Green light and says, "Ah, that's Yellow!" Your eye cannot tell the difference between the "real" yellow of the physical banana and the "fake" yellow of the screen, but a scientific instrument (like a spectrometer) would immediately see that the screen is faking it.

**3. The Rules of Mixing are Reversed**
Because emitting and reflecting are physical opposites, the math of how you mix colors is literally reversed. 
*   **Reflecting (Subtractive):** When you mix paints, you are adding more materials that *absorb* (subtract) light. If you mix enough paint colors together, they absorb almost all the light, leaving you with black/dark brown.
*   **Emitting (Additive):** When you mix light on a screen, you are *adding* more energy. If you mix all the colors of light together, you get pure, blinding white.

**Summary**
You are entirely right that the *end result*—light hitting the eye and triggering color—is the same. But the "emit vs. reflect" difference is the reason why mixing green and red paint makes brown, while mixing green and red light makes yellow!

It is completely understandable why you would think that, because that is exactly what we are all taught in grade school! 

When science teachers teach us about color, they focus on reflection because it applies to 99% of the physical things we interact with every day: our clothes, the grass, the walls, our food. For everyday survival and navigating the physical world, "color = reflected light" is a perfectly practical rule of thumb.

But in the grander scheme of physics, reflection isn't the "general rule" of color. It is actually just one item on a long list of ways nature creates color. 

The *true* general rule of science is simply this: **Color is just different wavelengths of light.** How those wavelengths get to your eye doesn't matter. 

In fact, if we look closely at nature, we find that screens aren't using an "engineering workaround" at all. They are just mimicking other natural ways light behaves. Here are a few examples of natural color that have absolutely nothing to do with reflection:

**1. The Original Source (Emission)**
Before light can bounce off an apple, it has to come from somewhere. The Sun, fire, and bioluminescent animals (like fireflies or deep-sea jellyfish) create color through **emission**. The sun doesn't *reflect* yellow/white light; it creates it through nuclear fusion. If emission is just a workaround, then the Sun itself is a workaround! Without emitted light, reflected light cannot exist.

**2. The Sky is Blue (Scattering)**
There is no blue paint or blue object in the sky reflecting light. The sky is blue because of **scattering**. When sunlight hits the gases in our atmosphere, the physical size of the gas molecules catches the short, blue wavelengths of light and scatters them in every direction like a pinball machine. 

**3. Rainbows (Refraction)**
A rainbow isn't a physical object reflecting light. It is caused by **refraction**. When sunlight passes through a raindrop, the water acts like a prism, bending the light and splitting it apart into its individual wavelengths. 

**4. Peacock Feathers and Butterflies (Structural Color)**
This is one of the coolest tricks in nature. A peacock feather actually has no blue or green pigment in it at all. If you grind up a peacock feather, it turns into a dull brown powder. The vivid colors come from microscopic, 3D crystalline structures in the feather that bounce light waves into each other, amplifying some colors and canceling out others (called **interference**). 

**The Verdict**
Your science teachers weren't lying to you; they were just giving you the "everyday objects" version of the story so you wouldn't have to learn quantum physics in the 4th grade! 

Reflection is the most common way we experience color when we touch things. But screens emitting light aren't breaking the rules of nature—they are just using the exact same physics as the Sun, a flame, or a firefly.
